core: Language as a core carrier of culture and identity, distributed unevenly across space

Language families as groups of related languages descended from a common ancestor (proto-language), and the language-tree model of branches and subgroups; major families named neutrally (Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan, Niger-Congo, Afro-Asiatic, Austronesian)
Dialects, accent vs dialect, and the fuzzy, partly political language/dialect distinction (mutual intelligibility is not a clean criterion)
Contact languages: lingua franca, pidgin (no native speakers), and creole (a nativized, fully developed former pidgin)
Official languages (de jure vs de facto), language and identity/nationalism
Roughly 7,000 languages exist (estimates vary by source and by where the language/dialect line is drawn); a large, dated, attributed share are endangered or dying
supporting: The idea that all languages are equally valid, rule-governed systems; there are no 'primitive' vs 'advanced' languages
Uneven spatial distribution of linguistic diversity (Asia and Africa hold the most languages; Europe far fewer)
outOfScope: Culture as the umbrella concept (owned by the culture topic; referenced only)
Ethnicity and religion as identity markers (named but owned by their own topics)
Technical linguistics: phonology, syntax, and formal historical-linguistic reconstruction methods in depth

claims.claim: A language family is a group of related languages that share features of pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammar and have descended from a common ancestral language, or proto-language; families are subdivided into branches and subgroups, a hierarchy often pictured as a language tree.

Linguistic diversity is unevenly distributed across space: by region, Asia has roughly 2,300 languages and Africa about 2,100, while Europe has only a few hundred; the Indo-European family alone is the first language of nearly half the world's population, and Sino-Tibetan (chiefly the Chinese languages) has well over a billion speakers.

The line between a language and a dialect is not purely linguistic: mutually intelligible varieties are sometimes counted as separate languages for political or historical reasons (e.g., Swedish and Danish), while varieties that are not mutually intelligible are sometimes grouped under one language name (e.g., the Chinese 'dialects'). A common saying captures this: a language is a dialect with an army and navy.

A lingua franca is a language adopted as a common medium of communication and commerce among groups who do not share a native tongue (Swahili across much of East Africa; English increasingly worldwide). A pidgin is a simplified contact language with reduced vocabulary and grammar and no native speakers, arising from trade or contact (Tok Pisin in Papua New Guinea, drawn largely from English). When a pidgin's vocabulary and grammar expand and children acquire it as a first language, it becomes a creole.

An official language is one granted legal status for government use; status can be de jure (declared by law) or de facto (dominant in practice without a formal declaration). States may recognize one, several, or no official languages, and language choice is closely tied to national identity and can be a source of unity or of conflict.

The world has on the order of 7,000 languages, though totals vary by source and by where the language/dialect boundary is drawn: Ethnologue's 27th edition (2024) lists 7,164 living languages, while UNESCO refers to roughly 6,500. A large share are at risk: UNESCO states that no less than 40 percent of known languages are extinct or endangered, and 244 languages have become extinct since 1950; Ethnologue classifies well over 3,000 living languages (roughly 43 percent) as endangered.

All human languages are equally complex, rule-governed systems capable of expressing any idea; the notion of 'primitive' versus 'advanced' languages is rejected in linguistics and geography, which treat every language as a valid carrier of culture and identity.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many languages exist in the world.
positions: UNESCO refers to roughly 6,500 languages spoken today.
OER geography texts state estimates vary between about 5,000 and 7,000.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson gives the widely used round figure of about 7,000, names Ethnologue's specific 2024 count and UNESCO's lower estimate with dates and attribution, and explains that the spread itself follows from the fuzzy, partly political language/dialect boundary rather than from measurement error.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The share of languages that are endangered.
positions: UNESCO: no less than 40 percent of known languages are extinct or endangered; its Atlas covers about 2,700 languages.
Ethnologue (27th ed.): over 3,000 living languages, roughly 43 percent, are Endangered, and about 1,000 are Dying.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both authorities agree the share is large; the lesson reports 'roughly 40 percent or more' with each figure attributed and dated, and does not manufacture false precision.

Framed all languages as equally valid systems, adding an explicit correction of the 'primitive vs advanced' misconception, per the even-handed control.

sourceRecords.provider: David Dorrell & Joseph P. Henderson (University of North Georgia Press), via Social Sci LibreTexts
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports: language family defined as related languages sharing pronunciation/vocabulary/grammar and descended from a common proto-language; the branch/subgroup hierarchy (language-tree model); Indo-European as first language of nearly half the world's population; Sino-Tibetan ~1,197 million speakers; regional distribution (Asia ~2,300, Africa ~2,138 languages, Europe far fewer); dialects as variants of one language and the political/historical complications of the language/dialect line (Swedish/Danish; Chinese 'dialects'). Only facts used; all prose rewritten, so CC BY attribution (not reproduction) applies.

sourceRecords.title: Cultural Geography (C-ID GEOG 120), 4.05: Classification of Languages
sourceRecords.provider: Coalinga College, via Social Sci LibreTexts
sourceRecords.notes: Read via WebFetch. Supports: lingua franca as a shared medium of communication and commerce among groups without a common native tongue (Swahili in East Africa; English worldwide); pidgin as a composite language with simplified grammar and limited vocabulary from trade contact (Tok Pisin, English-derived, Papua New Guinea); creole as an expanded pidgin with larger vocabulary, more complex grammar, and native speakers; official language as a language with legal status, distinguishing de jure from de facto; dialect as variants of one language. Only facts used; prose rewritten; NonCommercial term does not restrict factual reuse.
